content:
We need to compare simulated spectra with observed.

Observed 13C NMR: Deltas: 147.00, 133.90, 128.91 (x2), 127.68 (x2), 44.06, 34.54 (x2), 26.90 (x2), 26.18.

Simulated: 134.30, 133.23, 131.35, 130.38, 127.70, 127.30, 125.60, 124.40, 36.40, 33.10, 23.20.

Not a great match. Observed has high 147 ppm (aryl C-Cl). Simulated lacks that. Also observed has many aromatic signals around 128-147, while simulated has many around 124-134 but not 147. Also number of carbons: observed 12 peaks (including duplicates) vs simulated 11 distinct signals (maybe 11 carbons?). Simulated shows 11 signals, but we have 12 carbons. So maybe our SMILES missing a carbon? Actually our SMILES has 12 carbons, but simulated gave 11 signals maybe due to symmetry merging.

The simulated 13C peaks: 134.30,133.23,131.35,130.38,127.70,127.30,125.60,124.40 (8 aromatic/sp2) and 36.40,33.10,23.20 (3 aliphatic). Observed had 4 aromatic distinct (147,133.9,128.9,127.68) and 4 aliphatic distinct (44.06,34.54,26.90,26.18). So mismatch.

Thus our proposed structure likely incorrect. Need to reconsider.

Observed aromatic carbon at 147 ppm suggests a carbon attached to electronegative substituent like Cl or O (aryl C-Cl ~ 130-140? Actually C-Cl ~ 130-140, C-O ~ 150-160). 147 could be aryl carbon attached to O (phenoxy) or carbonyl? But we have no O in formula. So C-Cl maybe 140-145. So aromatic chlorine present.

Other aromatic carbons at 133.9, 128.9, 127.68 typical phenyl.

Aliphatic carbon at 44.06 likely carbon attached to Cl (C-Cl sp3 ~ 40-50). So chlorine may be on aliphatic carbon, not aromatic. That suggests formula C12H14Cl with chlorine on aliphatic carbon (44 ppm) and aromatic ring unsubstituted (no Cl). But then why 147 ppm? Could be a carbonyl (C=O) ~ 170, not 147. Could be aromatic carbon attached to something electron withdrawing like C=C? 147 could be alkene carbon attached to phenyl (styrene). Indeed styrene carbon (C=) appears around 145-150 ppm. So maybe we have a phenyl attached to an alkene (C=C). So structure could be a chlorinated alkyl chain attached to phenyl via double bond.

Consider structure: 4-chlorostyrene? That would be C8H7Cl, not enough carbons.

Our formula C12H14Cl could be a chlorinated alkylbenzene with an internal double bond (alkene). Example: 1-chloro-1-phenylhex-2-ene? Let's think.

If we have phenyl attached to an alkene carbon (C=) that is also attached to chlorine? That carbon would be sp2 attached to Cl and phenyl, chemical shift ~140-150. The other alkene carbon (CH) would be ~130 ppm. That matches 147 and 133.9.

Aliphatic carbons: 44 (C-Cl sp3) maybe not needed if Cl already on alkene carbon. But we have 44, maybe a carbon bearing Cl sp3 elsewhere.

But we only have one Cl. So either Cl on aromatic (C-Cl ~ 130) or on sp2 carbon (C-Cl sp2 ~ 140) or sp3 carbon (C-Cl sp3 ~ 40). Observed both 147 (sp2) and 44 (sp3) suggests maybe two chlorines? But formula only one Cl. So maybe 44 is not C-Cl but a carbon adjacent to aromatic (benzylic) ~ 40-45. Yes benzylic carbon (CH2 attached to phenyl) appears ~35-45. So 44 could be benzylic CH2.

Thus structure: phenyl-CH2-CH=CH-CH2-CH2-CH3 with a chlorine somewhere? Wait we need Cl somewhere else? Actually we have only one Cl, maybe on aromatic ring (C-Cl ~ 147). Then benzylic CH2 at 44. That fits: aromatic carbon bearing Cl at 147, other aromatic carbons 133.9,128.9,127.68. Benzylic CH2 attached to phenyl (44). Remaining aliphatic chain carbons: 34.54, 26.90, 26.18 typical for alkyl chain.

Thus structure could be chlorobenzyl alkane: e.g., 4-chlorobenzylbutane? Let's compute formula: chlorobenzyl (C7H6Cl) + butyl (C4H9) = C11H15Cl? Not 12 carbons.

We need total 12 carbons: phenyl ring 6, plus side chain 6. Side chain includes benzylic CH2 (attached to phenyl) plus 5 more carbons. So overall C12H14Cl.

If chlorine is on aromatic ring, phenyl becomes C6H4Cl (since one H replaced). Then side chain C6H10 (alkyl). Total H =4 +10 =14. Good. So structure: chlorophenyl-alkyl chain (no other hetero). The benzylic carbon (attached to phenyl) is CH2 (44 ppm). The chain is saturated (no double bonds). Then aliphatic carbons typical 34, 26, etc.

Thus propose SMILES: Clc1ccccc1CCCCCC? Wait need 6 carbon chain attached to phenyl via CH2. So phenyl-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH3 (hexyl). That's chlorobenzylhexane? Actually phenyl-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH3 is phenylhexane (C12H16). With chlorine on ring, formula C12H14Cl (since phenyl loses 2 H? Wait phenyl with Cl has C6H4Cl, side chain C6H10, total H14). Yes.

SMILES: Clc1ccccc1CCCCCC? Need to attach chain to phenyl via CH2: The phenyl carbon attached to chain is part of ring; we need to specify substituent at position 1: Clc1ccccc1CCCCCC? That attaches chain to same carbon as Cl? Actually that would have both Cl and chain on same carbon, which would be disubstituted aromatic carbon (C bearing both Cl and chain) which would reduce H count by 2 (since that carbon originally had H, now has Cl and chain). That would give C6H3Cl-alkyl, total H =3 +10 =13, not 14. So chlorine must be on a different aromatic carbon than the chain attachment. So we need a para- or meta- substituted phenyl with Cl and alkyl.

Simplify: Use SMILES: Clc1ccc(cc1)CCCCCC? That is chlorophenyl with hexyl at para? Actually "Clc1ccc(cc1)CCCCCC" attaches hexyl to the aromatic carbon after the ring closure? The pattern: "c1ccc(cc1)" is phenyl. Prepending "Cl" attaches Cl to first carbon. Then after the ring, "CCCCCC" attaches to the same carbon as the last aromatic atom? Actually SMILES: "Clc1ccc(cc1)CCCCCC" means Cl attached to aromatic carbon 1, and the chain attached to the aromatic carbon after the ring closure (the same as the last aromatic atom). That gives two substituents on adjacent positions? Might be okay.

But we need only one Cl and one alkyl substituent on ring, total 2 substituents. That's fine.

Thus SMILES: "Clc1ccc(cc1)CCCCCC". Let's count carbons: aromatic 6, chain 6 =12. Hydrogens: aromatic with two substituents has 4 H left (since each substituent replaces H). So phenyl H =4. Chain C6H13? Actually hexyl attached via CH2 to ring: chain is -CH2-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH3 = C6H13. Total H =4+13=17, too many. Wait chain attached via CH2, the carbon attached to ring is CH2 (two H). So chain formula C6H13. So total H =4+13=17, not 14. Something off.

Our side chain should be C6H10 (saturated chain attached via CH2 but with two fewer H because aromatic carbon lost H? Actually aromatic carbon originally had H, replaced by chain, so chain carbon attached to ring is CH2 (2 H). That's fine. The chain length of 5 carbons beyond that CH2 gives total C6H13. So total H =4 (aryl) +13 =17. But formula needed H14. So chain must be less saturated (maybe contains a double bond reducing H by 2). If chain has one double bond, H reduces by 2 to C6H11, total H =4+11=15. Still one extra. Need H14, so chain must have two degrees unsaturation (e.g., double bond + maybe ring). But we have no other DBE besides aromatic (4) and maybe one double bond in chain (makes DBE 5). Need DBE 6, so chain must have two DBE (e.g., double bond + another double bond or ring). But observed aliphatic carbons are sp3, not unsaturated.

Thus maybe chlorine is on aromatic, chain is C6H9 (one double bond). That would give H =4 +9 =13, still low. Wait need 14. Let's compute: aromatic with Cl (C6H4Cl) has 4 H. Chain C6H10 (saturated) gives total H14. So chain must be saturated C6H10 attached via CH2 (makes sense). But we earlier got H total 17 because we counted aromatic H incorrectly: aromatic with two substituents has 4 H, correct. Chain C6H10 has 10 H. Total 14. Good! Wait chain C6H10 is not hexyl (C6H13). Hexyl is C6H13. So chain must be C6H10 meaning it has two degrees unsaturation (e.g., cyclohexyl). Indeed cyclohexyl (C6H11) is saturated ring, but attached via one bond reduces H by 1 => C6H11? Actually cyclohexyl radical C6H11 (C6H11). That's 11 H, not 10. So need C6H10 maybe cyclohexene (C6H10) attached via double bond? But then unsaturation.

Thus maybe side chain is cyclohexane attached via a carbon (cyclohexyl) gives C6H11, total H =4+11=15. Not match.

Thus our earlier assumption of saturated chain is inconsistent with formula.

Let's compute formula for chlorophenyl + cyclohexane (C6H11) = C12H15Cl. Too many H.

Chlorophenyl + cyclohexene (C6H9) = C12H13Cl. Too few H.

Thus need C6H10 side chain. Could be cyclohexyl with one double bond (cyclohexene) but attached via a carbon that loses H, giving C6H9? Hmm.

Maybe side chain is a propyl group attached to phenyl and also a chlorine on the chain, not on aromatic. That would give C12H14Cl with Cl on aliphatic carbon (44 ppm). Then aromatic carbon at 147 could be a carbonyl? Not.

But 147 could be aromatic carbon attached to something electron withdrawing like C=O (aryl carbonyl). But no O.

Maybe 147 is alkene carbon attached to phenyl (styrene). Indeed styrene carbon (C=) appears ~145 ppm. So aromatic carbon attached to alkene (Csp2) appears ~145. So 147 could be the alkene carbon attached to phenyl (C=). The other alkene carbon at 133.9. So we have a phenyl-alkene moiety (styrene). Then chlorine attached to benzylic carbon (CH2) at 44 ppm? But benzylic CH2 is attached to phenyl, not chlorine. However chlorine could be on that CH2 (CH2Cl) which shifts to ~44 ppm. So structure: chloromethyl-styrene? e.g., ClCH2-CH=CH-Ph? That would be C9? Let's compute: phenyl C6H5, alkene CH=CH- (C2H2), CH2Cl (C1H2Cl). Total C9? Actually C6+2+1=9. Need 12 carbons, so need additional alkyl groups.

Maybe structure: 4-chlorostyrene with extra alkyl chain? This is getting messy.

Given time, maybe the correct SMILES is "Clc1ccc(cc1)C=CC". But that's C9.

Given the simulated spectra for our candidate didn't match, we need a better candidate. Could try to search similar SMILES via search_by_smiles using our current guess to see similar compounds? But we need a SMILES to search. Could use generic formula C12H14Cl and get isomers. Use obtain_isomers_from_molecular_formula.
Let's get isomers for C12H14Cl.
